newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition plans to usher in New Year with protests.
newsitem.headline: Opposition plans to usher in New Year with protests.

text.p: Serbia's pro-democracy movement planned a New Year's Eve extravaganza of rallies and parties with alarm clocks set to ring at midnight, as if time were running out for President Slobodan Milosevic.

Buoyed by Western solidarity and an apparent statement of support from dissident Yugoslav army officers, demonstrators protesting against election fraud hit the streets in the capital Belgrade on Monday for the 43rd straight day.

The protest wave, enduring in the teeth of police moves to drive demonstrators off main streets, is the most sustained popular push for democratisation in 50 years of leftist one-party rule in Serbian-led Yugoslavia.
Five-thousand Belgrade university students tried to march across the Sava River bridge on Monday but were blocked by police and forced to retreat into a pedestrian mall.

Later, tens of thousands of people backing the Zajedno (Together) opposition party coalition massed in Republic Square with riot police packing adjacent streets to prevent protesters swarming into traffic zones.
Up to a quarter of a million people have rallied daily in Serbia against Milosevic's annulment of November 17 municipal elections in 14 cities, including Belgrade, won by Zajedno.

The ruling Socialists (SPS) cited "irregularities" in the vote. But Zajedno, supported later by findings of a special OSCE mission, accused the SPS of blatant vote fraud and demanded that its victories be reinstated.
Zajedno prepared a street spectacle for Tuesday, New Year's Eve, to keep up the enthusiasm of supporters whose ranks have dwindled since subzero, snowy weather set in a week ago.
A costume ball for children was scheduled followed by a midtown procession in mid-evening and then a huge party in Republic Square with well-known pop music groups and actors.
Zajedno said "tickets" for the party would consist of candles, sparklers or alarm clocks timed to go off at the stroke of 12 in a humorous warning to strongman Milosevic.

Serbian police banned street marches after a December 24 riot involving Zajedno protesters and government loyalists bused into Belgrade from the provinces to champion the beleaguered Serbian president.
The reclusive Milosevic is now mulling how to respond to last week's critical report by a delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Western governments have warned Milosevic he can forget about financial aid for Yugoslavia's wrecked economy unless he concedes electoral losses and starts broad democratic reform.
Dejan Bulatovic, a Zajedno activist, was released on Monday after serving 25 days in jail for carrying an effigy of Milosevic, the independent news agency Beta said.

Zajedno received a potentially important expression of support in a letter from what appeared to be disaffected officers in the Yugoslav Army (VJ). An army statement issued later denied any internal split over the demonstrations.
The letter, read out before 50,000 Zajedno activists in Belgrade on Sunday, warned Milosevic that the VJ authors would refuse to fire on demonstrators if ordered to do so.
The letter was addressed to Milosevic, VJ commander General Momcilo Perisic and pro-democracy university students in Nis, Serbia's second largest city, but not to Zajedno.
Zajedno was warned by the authors that the opposition would be toppled in its turn if it became autocratic in power.
It was unclear how many VJ officers might be involved in the letter, which was unsigned and unauthenticated.
The letter suggested that any move by Milosevic to declare a state of emergency would collapse.
The VJ statement released on Monday stressed army unity but omitted any pledge of loyalty to Milosevic.
Soldiers helped Milosevic crush demonstrations in 1991, but the VJ has stayed neutral during his conflict with Zajedno.
Perisic pledged during a meeting with Yugoslav federal president Zoran Lilic to preserve stability, the official news agency Tanjug said, without mentioning the officers' letter.
